qualifying_conditions: agent_type=hepatotoxic_metabolite | liver_injury_identifier=UMLS:C0235378 | qualifying_conditions=Elevated 6-MMPR concentrations in patients on thiopurine (6MP/AZA) therapy; most patients with elevated 6-MMPR have normal liver biochemistries. | extra_details=6-MMPR >5700 pmol/8×10^8 RBC reported to increase risk of hepatotoxicity (Dubinsky); increasing 6-MMPR correlated with ALT rises (Nygaard); Goldenberg found 12% of thiopurine patients had elevated 6-MMPR but none had liver chemistry abnormalities. 6-MMPR (and 6-TGN) testing considered low predictive value for hepatotoxicity monitoring, mainly identifying noncompliers; combination thiopurine-allopurinol therapy lowered 6-MMPR and normalized transaminases (Sparrow). | needs_more_context=False
support_text: Elevated 6-MMPR (6-methylmercaptopurine ribonucleotide) concentrations have been associated with hepatotoxicity: Dubinsky et al. reported increased risk of hepatotoxicity with 6-MMPR >5700 pmol/8×10^8 RBC, and Nygaard et al. found increasing 6-MMPR levels correlated with rises in alanine aminotransferase. However, elevated 6-MMPR is expected in many patients on 6MP or AZA, most have normal liver biochemistries, and Goldenberg et al. found 12% of patients on thiopurines had 6-MMPR >5700 without any liver chemistry abnormalities. The paper therefore presents both positive and negative hepatotoxicity evidence for elevated 6-MMPR without resolving them.
